sentences.text: The name Nannopterygius translates to "small wing or flipper" in Greek.
This creature grew to a maximum length of 3.5 meters.
Its head measured 50 centimeters in length and ended in a long, narrow snout.
Large eyes protected by a bony scleral ring were a defining trait of its family.
At least 60 disc-shaped vertebrae allowed for flexibility and agility in the water.
Unlike its relative Ophthalmosaurus, it possessed much smaller paddles, with forepaddles measuring 25 to 30 centimeters and hindpaddles only 10 to 15 centimeters.
Its streamlined, torpedo-shaped body made it an inefficient long-distance swimmer but capable of speed over short distances.
Scientists suggest it may have been an ambush predator that quickly plunged into shoals of fish in shallow seas.
The first specimen was discovered in the Kimmeridge Clay Formation of Dorset, UK, and described by Hulke in 1871 as Ichthyosaurus enthekiodon.
Friedrich von Huene established the genus Nannopterygius in 1922, naming it after the animal's small paddles.
In 2020, several new species were named based on fossils found in Norway and Russia.
Two additional species from Kazakhstan were confirmed in 2022.
This animal belongs to the family Ophthalmosauridae.
An analysis by Zverkov and Jacobs in 2020 identified it as the sister taxon to Thalassodraco within Ophthalmosauria.
Nannopterygius lived during the Late Jurassic periods of the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian.
It existed between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
Fossils have been found in England, Kazakhstan, Russia, and Norway.
During the Late Jurassic, Europe was an island archipelago surrounded by warm, tropical seas.
The Kimmeridge Clay Formation represents an offshore marine environment where the seafloor was deep enough to avoid storm disturbance.
The species N. yasykovi and N. saveljeviensis are found in the Volga region of Russia, which defines the Volgian stage.
The species N. borealis is known from earliest Cretaceous sediments in the Slottsmøya Member of the Agardhfjellet Formation.
The seafloor at the Slottsmøya site was located about 150 meters below the surface and was relatively oxygen-poor.
The Slottsmøya Member contains fossils of other marine reptiles such as Undorosaurus, Arthropterygius, and Brachypterygius alongside Nannopterygius.
